325.text: Pettibone (1967) synonymised two species of Admetella described by Chamberlin (1919) - A. hastigerens and A. dolichopus - with A. longipedata McIntosh 1885. However, she examined a number of specimens from Hawaii, Philippine Islands, and Baja California which had originally been designated/identified as A. hastigerens, A. dolichopus and Polynoe mirabilis sensu Treadwell (1906) for her re-description of A. longipedata, in which it is unclear which specimens she is referring to. Fauchald (1972) subsequently resurrected A. hastigerens by reason of the absence of chaetae on the tentaculophores which he states are present in A. longipedata and refers to McIntosh’s Figure 5, Plate 14; however, there are no chaetae visible on segment 1 in this figure of the dorsal view of the anterior end of A. longipedata, nor is there any mention of their presence in McIntosh’s description. Type specimens of A. hastigerens (and A. dolichopus) both have notochaetae absent (or all missing) reported in their original descriptions by Chamberlin, which distinguishes them from A. longipedata syntypes in which they are present (as reported by McIntosh), as they are in our specimens. As the type locality for A. hastigerens is Panama (off Coiba Is) in 1063 m water depth, and that of A. longipedata is east of Prince Edward Is, Antarctic Indian Ocean in 2515 m depth, the two widely geographically distant locations suggest that suggest the possibility of two different species, and records of A. longipedata from the Andaman Sea, Pater Noster Island, Indian Ocean and West Indies by Fauvel (1953) are likely incorrect, so that such specimens in the USNM would need to be re-examined to establish their true identity. Because there is currently little possibility of examining the type material of A.longipedata in NHM London, UK, and the fact that our specimens are so badly damaged, we are tentatively referring these specimens from SE Australian waters to this species. Kristian Fauchald examined some A. longipedata material in 2001, but it seems that his subsequent notes and description refer to non-type specimens from the Hawaiian Islands deposited in the USNM (ie not from the type locality), and again, this may not be a useful description to distinguish the species. The two syntypes are described by McIntosh (1885) as “upwards of sixty segments in the one and fifty in the other” and “all the scales are absent, but ..twenty-four pairs seem to have been present”. If the generic assignment here is correct this is first molecular sequence data available for a member of the Admetellinae

325.text: Despite the absence of posterior segments and pygidium, this specimen agrees with the generic diagnosis for Anotochaetonoe, including the irregular distribution of elytra after segment 23, the presence of a row of parapodial papillae next to the ventral cirri, and the presence of bidentate neurochaetae (cf. Lepidasthenia, Telolepidasthenia and Alentiana, all of which have unidentate neurochaetae). There has been only one species of Anotochaetonoe described so far, A. michelbhaudii Britayev & Martin 2005, from the Atlantic Ocean, off Republic of Congo, Africa, in 70–180 m depth, associated with chaetopterid tubes, and also more recently from Gulf of Cadiz, off the Iberian penisula, in 228 m depth, associated with an onuphid tube (Ravara et al, 2017). Our specimen came from off northern NSW, in 1194 m depth, from a sample that included the onuphid Hyalinoecia abranchiata Lechapt 1997, (Gunton et al., 2021), and is therefore from a geographically widely distant oceanic basin. It differs from A. michelbhaudii by a number of minor features: it lacks knob-like tips on the superior neurochaetae, which are blunt only; micropapillae are absent from elytra which also lack light brown pigmentation arranged in polygonal units in anterior part of elytra; small red-brown pigment spots are present, scattered on parapodia, elytra and cirri; ventral parapodial papillae lack ciliation; and much smaller eyes than A. michelbhaudi.

40.text: Antipathypolyeunoa is one of many genera in the family Polynoidae which have an obligate commensal relationship with a host marine invertebrate. As the name suggests, species of Antipathypolyeunoa are associated with antipatharian corals, being found in hollow tubes in the main stems of the coral host.

325.text: Antipathipolyeunoa Pettibone 1991 are long-bodied Polynoinae; they are distinguished from other genera with numerous segments and more than 40 pairs of elytra by having ventrally inserted lateral antennae, cephalic peaks and a subacicular neuropodial lobe. The genus now comprises two species including Antipathipolyeunoa xxxx sp nov described below from the Great Australian Bight in the Southern Ocean and A. nuttingi Pettibone 1991 from the North Atlantic. Serpetti et al. 2017 reported material of Antipathipolyeunoa from the Indian Ocean but did not describe a new species

This form was indeed new at the time when Pruvot was studying it (1905) but his notes, his drawings, as well as the examination of the still existing material, leave no doubt that it is Austrolaenilla antarctica described by Bergström in 1916. Pruvot's notes being unpublished, it is appropriate to adopt the specific name of Bergström, but recently Monro (1929, p. 62 and 1930, p. 67) contested the usefulness of the genus Austrolaenilla which is really synonym of Antinoë." (Fauvel, 1932: 9) and "Specimens 307, 384, and 396, which Pruvot referred to as Laenilla fulgens, differ from the others only by their ventral bristles a little less tapering and less feathery at the tip. There is also a little less difference between the upper dorsal bristles and lower. The head, feet and elytra are similar (Pl. I, figs. 11-13). There is therefore no need to make two distinct species of them; at the most we could keep a fulgens Pruvot variety because these differences are really very minimal, as we can see by examining the figures on Plate 1." 325.text: The small size of the specimens (30–35 segments, compared with ~ 40+ segments for Austrolaenilla species) indicates that they may be juvenile, but the identification is based on the diagnostic features for the genus: the presence of neurochaetae more slender than notochaetae, and with capillary tips that terminate distally in tufts of fine hairs, which these specimens possess. There are ten currently valid Austrolaenilla species (Read and Fauchald 2020), some of which have been described and reported from southern Antarctic and New Zealand waters, but we are unwilling to attempt a more specific identification due to the small and probably juvenile nature of the specimens. Neither specimen generated a COI sequence but 16S and 18S sequences have been deposited on Genbank (xxxx) and may allow description of this species when additional material is collected.

325.text: Bathybahamas Pettibone, 1985 has 18 segments and 8 pairs of elytra. In total seven genera of Macellicephalinae have only 8 pairs of elytra and all also lack lateral antennae. Among these, Bathybahamas is unique in having eyes and in having neurochaetae which are not flattened or spatulate but instread cylindrical in cross-section, with capillary tips. A single described species of Bathybahamas is currently known, B. charleneae Pettibone, 1985, which is short-bodied and occurs in the North Atlantic Ocean off the Bahamas at a depths of 2066 m.

325.text: Anna comments "This is probably a species of Bathybahamas, because of the number of segments (18) and pairs of elytra (8), lack of lateral antennae, tentaculophores with a projecting acicular process and lacking chaetae, short, cirriform dorsal tubercles on the non-elytragenous segments, and the forms of the notochaetae and neurochaetae. However, the specimens both possess notopodia subequal in length to neuropodia, while the only species in this genus, Bathybahamas charlenae Pettibone 1985, typically possesses notopodia shorter than neuropodia, and as our specimens are also too damaged and fragile to attempt to dissect out the jaws and pharynx to determine the number of pharyngeal papillae (in Bathybahamas, 7 pairs) & jaw type (in Bathybahamas, 2 non-dentate pairs), we cannot determine whether this is a new species or not." Robin comments "Possibly not Bathybahamas which has eyes and has neurochaetae with capillary tips. Possible genera (with 8 pairs elytra and lateral antennae absent) together with characters that separate within this group are: Bathybahamas Pettibone, 1985 [Segment 2 interrupted, not visible dorsal view; simple neurochaetae with capillary tips present; nuchal flap absent] Bathyeliasona Pettibone, 1976 [tentaculophores with chaetae; Frontal filaments present; prostomium anterior margin comprising apair of acute anterior projections] Bathypolaria Levenstein, 1981 [Ventral keel of posterior end present] Bathyvitiazia Pettibone, 1976 [Number pairs of terminal papillae on pharynx: 6] Bruunilla Hartman, 1971 [ventrum with a pair of tapering wing-like structures projecting laterally] Macellicephaloides Uschakov, 1955 [ventrum with a deep pit on segment 2 covered by a large flap attached to segment 3] Yodanoe Bonifácio & Menot, 2018 [Prostomium anterior margin comprising a pair of acute anterior projections; tentaculophores without chaetae; Number pairs of terminal papillae on pharynx: 9; cephalic peaks absent]. RW new comment July 2022: I've compared this again with the revised generic diagnoses (DELTA is upgraded) and yes, Bathybahamas is closest home for this species. (Can't be Bruunilla since it lacks the ventral wing-like structures on segment 3.) However generic diagnosis will have to be emended to include eyes absent and remove "neurochaetae with capillary tips"

325.text: The specimen is damaged and fragile, and most notochaetae and all elytra are missing. Two genera share the characters which distinguish our specimen (10 pairs of elytra, median and lateral antennae absent): Bathyedithia and Polaruschakov. Both genera also have similar neurochaetae, which are flattened and serrated on both margins. Bathyedithia has seven or nine pairs of terminal papillae on the pharynx compared with Polaruschakov which has 14 pairs (Pettibone 1976) but we have been unable to observe this character on our single fragile and damaged specimen. On the basis of the presence of dentate lateral margins of the jaws (and which are absent from Polaruschakov species) this specimen was assigned to Bathyedithia

325.text: Austropolaria was originally described as a monotypic genus, based on A. magnicirrata described by Neal et al. (2012) from 1000–1500 m in the Amundsen Sea of the Antarctic region. These specimens agree closely with this species diagnosis including that the pharynx has seven pairs of terminal papillae, nine pairs of reduced elytrophores, large dorsal cirrophores, and a posterior ventral keel. Kolbasova et al. (2020) showed after molecular analysis that the monotypic genus Austropolaria is a junior synonym of Bathypolaria Levenstein, 1981, and emended the generic diagnosis for Bathypolaria to include a variable range of segments (13–20) and elytrophores (7–9). As many Macellicephalinae genera and species have been diagnosed based on a fixed number of such morphological characters, it would appear that these may have to be revisited once material can be sequenced for these species and (particularly) monotypic genera erected by Pettibone

325.text: Bathytasmania Levenstein, 1982 is one of 4 genera of Macellicephalinae with 10 pairs of elytra, the others being Bathycanadia Levenstein, 1981, Bathyedithia Pettibone, 1976, Polaruschakov Pettibone, 1976 and Vampiropolynoe Marcus & Hourdez, 2002. Bathytasmania is distinguished from these by having the last two pairs of elytra on consecutive segments and having notochaetal spines with capillary tips. Bathytasmania includes a single species, B. insolita Levenstein, 1982 from a depth of 4395 metres in the Southern Ocean, south of Tasmania, Australia.

325.text: Only two genera of Polynoidae are known to have notochaetae and neurochaetae with semilunar pockets: Benhamisetosus Averincev, 1978 and Subadyte Pettibone, 1969. Benhamisetosus was established by Averincev (1978) for Scalisetosus australiensis Benham, 1915 because the neurochaetae of Benham's species have semilunar pockets which excludes the species from Scalisetosus (see Pettibone, 1969). Benhamisetosus australiensis is known only from Benham's original specimen and 4 specimens reported by Averincev (1978) but all material is incomplete; the genus is still monotypic. Based on the available information the two genera are separated by the antennae which have papillate styles in Benhamisetosus but are smooth in species of Subadyte, and presence of a facial tubercle in Benhamisetosus which is lacking in species of Subadyte. These are characters which are variable between species in many other genera. Given the poor condition of all material of Benhamisetosus the genus should probably be made a synonym of Subadyte Pettibone 1969. Although currently considered Polynoidae incertae sedis, Benhamisetosus (if retained) should probably be placed in the Polynoinae based on the insertion of the lateral antennae and on the neurochaetae with semilunar pockets, which only occur in Adyte Saint-Joseph, 1899 and Subadyte, both placed in Polynoinae

325.text: Bruunilla Hartman, 1971 was described for a single species, B. natalensis Hartman, 1971 from abyssal depths in the Indian Ocean. However, it was Pettibone (1979) who redescribed B. natalensis and recognised that the genus as a polynoid. The generic description was emended and a second species was described from the abyssal Pacific Ocean by Bonifácio & Menot (2018); those authors also reported additional genetic diversity representing additional distinct but undescribed species in the Pacific Ocean. Although the placement of Bruunilla within the polychaetes was originally unclear, intact specimens are readily recognised due to the large paired wing-like structures covering the ventrum of the first three segments. The generic description above is based on Bonifácio & Menot (2018). Including the two new species described below, Bruunilla now includes four described species.

324.text: Paratype 4 mm long, 1 mm wide (excluding parapodia), with 18 segments (including pygidium). Specimen also has small prostomium, but with 2 large median antenna ceratophores (aberrant) in U-shaped notch between prostomial lobes, arising from between the middle of the prostomial lobes, styles missing; anterior margins of prostomial lobes with minute frontal filaments. Upper lip with 2 small low lobes. Dorsal cirri, tentacular cirri and antennal style(s) all missing; some ventral cirri present; buccal cirrophore scar large, located basally on neuropodia, subsequent ventral cirri evenly tapering, long, smooth, attached subdistally anteriorly then medially from mid-body segments (chaetiger 9). Parapodia longer than body width. Neuropodia with small ventral patches of ctenidia in a line from body to distal end of neuropodium. Posterior end somewhat damaged, but elongate papillae appear to be absent/missing from posterior neuropodia. Chaetae similar to holotype

325.text: This species is morphologically similar to Bruunilla posteroantennata sp. nov. except that there are fewer body segments -18 compared with 17- the prostomium is much smaller, and with a large protruding bulbous median antenna ceratophore (albeit with style missing) arising from between the middle of lobes of prostomium (not small and arising posteriorly as in B. posteroanntenata); ventral cirri attached medially in mid to posterior segments; a lower lip that has two small low lobes (not trilobed as in Bruunilla posteroantennata) and the mostly longitudinal folding of the ventral lamellate lobes. This species also differs from B. nealae Bonifácio & Menot 2018 by the lack of elongate neuropodial papillae on segments 11–14, the form and position on the prostomium of the median antennal ceratophore, the longitudinal folding of the ventral lamellate lobes, as well as the more medially arising ventral cirri. Bonifácio & Menot (2018) were unable to obtain CO1 sequences for B. nealae, however 16S data (16S_ML_Abyssal_23Aug21.pdf) show that the 4 specimens of Bruunilla reported here represent 2 species, both distinct from Bruunilla nealae.

Median antenna ceratophore small, inserted posteriorly in anterior notch. Ovoid frontal filament present on one side, other presumed missing. Ventral cirri inserted near middle of neuropodia; buccal cirri longer than subsequent ventral cirri; dorsal cirri similar to holotype. 325.text: Morphological differences between Bruunilla posteroantennata sp. nov. and B. nealae Bonifácio & Menot 2018, include the median antenna inserted more posteriorly on prostomium; ventral cirri inserted mid-neuropodium (reportedly subdistal in B. nealae); and the lack of elongate neuropodial papillae on segments 11–14 (present in B. nealae). This species is also morphologically dissimilar to the type species for the genus, B. natalensis Hartman 1971, which possesses ventral wing-like structures that are tapered laterally and posteriorly (not rounded) and lacks frontal filaments. It also differs from Bruunilla magnantennata sp. nov. by the form and position on the prostomium of the median antenna (small & posteriorly placed compared with large and anteriorly placed in B. magnantennata); a trilobed lower lip (compared with 2 low lobes); and the different orientation of the folding of ventral lamellate lobes (mostly horizontal in this species compared with mostly longitudinal in B. magnantennata). Bonifácio & Menot (2018) were unable to obtain CO1 sequences for B. nealae, however 16S data (16S_ML_Abyssal_23Aug21.pdf) indicate that the 4 specimens of Bruunilla reported here represent 2 species, both distinct from Bruunilla nealae.

324.text: Other paratypes display pigmentation on cephalic peaks and prostomium, and dark violet-brown pigment dorsally and ventrally; some have a violet/brown-pigmented anal segment. The number of posterior segments without pigment (i.e. white) varies between 5 and 10. Tentaculophores may have up to 2 chaetae per side. Pygidial appendages are also highly variable - some specimens have a single long cirrus with an anal flap/funnel arising ventrally from pygidial segment (Fig. J), or 2 long pygidial cirri with a long ventral anal flap. The non-type specimens from Flat Maatsuyker, Tasmania, have up to 72 segments and may either lack pigment, or have up to 25 posteriormost segments without pigment.

325.text: Some specimens of this species cannot easily be morphologically distinguished from Eunoe leiotentaculata, if they lack the characteristic “white-tail”, which some longer specimens from the Tasmanian Flat Maatsuyker area appear to do. If elytra are present (not missing) then the characteristic crescent-shaped pigment pattern on those of E. leiotentaculata may help to distinguish it from this species. It differs from other Eunoe spp. by a combination of characters such as the presence of large eyes, the lack of papillae on antennae and cirri, the form of ornamentation (papillae and microtubercles) and “pearly” lustre of the elytra, the ornamentation on and form of the tips of the neurochaetae, as well as posterior segments of the body lacking pigment altogether. COI was obtained from 3 of the 4 specimens sequenced, generating intra-clade uncorrected p-distances less than 0.01%. Eunoe "whitetail" was found to be closely related ( uncorrected COI p-distances 0.1%) to Neopolynoe acanellae (Verrill, 1882) from 760 m in the northeast Atlantic Ocean (Taboada et al., 2019).

325.text: These specimens do not exactly agree with any descriptions of the 46 valid species of Eunoe, particularly most of those that have been reported from southern Australian, New Zealand and Antarctic waters, i.e., E. opalina, E. abyssorum, E. leiotentaculata Averincev, 1978, E. papillaris Averincev, 1978, E. ivantsovi Averincev, 1978, E. iphionoides McIntosh, 1885, and E. campbellica Averincev, 1978. There are differences such as elytral ornamentation and form of the neurochaetae. The most similar species is E. etheridgei Benham, 1915, with which our specimens share features such as papillate antennal and dorsal cirri styles, ornamentation of notochaetae, and notochaetae thicker than neurochaetae, but which differs from descriptions of E. etheridgei by the ornamentation of elytra (E. etheridgei possesses 'conical tubercles', a marginal fringe of long papillae and long 'finger-shaped papillae' near the posterior margin of the elytra – these last two are features which these specimens lack), the presence of minute papillae on long palps and the broad, almost flattened shape of the neurochaetae tips. Eunoe etheridgei was recorded from Bass Strait at only 360 m. Polynoinae sp. 5 from the GAB surveys in 426– 1027 m depth may be the same as Eunoe sp. 3 (MacIntosh et al. 2018: additional file 2) COI sequences from 2 specimens generated uncorrected p-distance of 0.7%.

All elytra missing from both specimens and some chaetigers have also been removed (by Benham?). These specimens also show some variability: eyes, if present, are subdermal and not obvious; 0–1 chaetae may be present on the tentacular segment. Elytra are fragile and thin, often degraded on posterior and external margins. AM W.53618 (sequenced, largest specimen): posteriorly incomplete, with 26 segments for 32 mm long, 11 mm wide (excluding chaetae), nephridial papillae obvious from segment 10, elytra all eroded and ragged on external and posterior edges, microtubercles present on anterior areas, papillae absent. Another specimens from same sample (AM W.53876, also sequenced), incomplete with palps present, long, smooth, reaching back to segment 7, with 2 pairs of small subdermal eyes also present, anterior pair at widest part of prostomium, posterior pair slightly more medial, both dorsally oriented, and with most elytra missing, those remaining degraded and ragged on external and posterior areas, microtubercles present, papillae absent. Specimen AM W.53859, complete, 36 mm long, 9 mm wide (excl. chaetae), with 41 chaetigers, 15 pairs elytra (most missing), last 9 posteriormost segments uncovered, 2 pairs faint eyes subdermally, cephalic peaks present, all antennal styles missing, tentacular segment with 1 chaeta on one side only, tentacular cirri long, upper lip trilobed. Elytra with microtubercles (some sharply conical) present on anterior and lateral areas and margin, papillae and macrotubercles absent (close-up photos taken).

325.text: In Benham’s (1921) description of these specimens (as E. abyssorum McIntosh 1885), he states that the lateral antennae "bear a few microscopic hairs", however we observed no papillae on the lateral antennae (nor tentacular cirri and dorsal cirri) which are all smooth; the ventral purple pigment has also faded completely, as have the eyes on the larger of the two paratype specimens. Benham also states that neurochaetae are "rather stouter than the largest of lower ones in the notopod", however, we observed that in general, noto- and neurochaetae were of similar thickness, and it was just a few of the inferior notochaetae that were smaller and thinner than the neurochaetae (see Fig). Because the type specimen of E.abyssorum is in poor condition and uninformative (dried out and lacking elytra), elsewhere in this paper we designate E. abyssorum McIntosh 1885 species inquirenda. Rather than cause possible further confusion by confirming these specimens as the same species as McIntosh’s, we have erected a new species for Benham’s specimens which he considered as the same species despite the obvious deficiencies of the existing type specimen. The specimens from Bass Strait and off southern NSW have the same elytral ornamentation and chaetal morphology as Benham’s specimens (see Figs) and we consider these specimens to belong to the same species. Maximum intra-clade genetic distance for E. benhami sp. nov. is 0.8% (uncorrected COI p-distance); corresponding inter-clade distances from the most similar species, Harmothoe paxtoni (from this study) and Eunoe bathydomus (from the North Atlantic) are 4.2% and 7.3% respectively. Eunoe benhami sp. nov. can be distinguished from other bathyal and abyssal Polynoidae using the key provided here. Eunoe benhami sp. nov. is most likely to be confused with Harmothoe paxtoni but apart from lacking soft elytral mounds characteristic of H. paxtoni and lacking bidentate neurochaetae the new species also differs in lacking chaetae on the tentacular segment and lacking papillae on the lateral antennae ceratostyles. We discuss the close relationships between species of Eunoe and Harmothoe elsewhere in this paper. Eunoe benhami sp. nov. is similar to E. papillaris Averincev, 1978 but the latter species differs in having chaetae on the tentacular sgment, tentacular cirri lacking papillae, and anterior pair of eyes located posterior to the widest part of the prostomium

325.text: This species is similar to other Eunoe spp, but can be differentiated from them by a combination of features – the dark iridescent pigmented body, the lack of elytral macrotubercles and papillae (cf Eunoe leiotentaculata, Eunoe ivantsovi, Eunoe papillaris, Eunoe opalina, Eunoe iphionides, Eunoe etheridgei) and the lack of papillate antennae, tentacular cirri and dorsal cirri (cf Eunoe campbellica, E. iphionides, E. opalina, E. papillaris, E. etheridgei, Eunoe apicolata n. sp.) as well as the robust ornamentation and strongly curved tips of the neurochaetae (cf E. apicolata n.sp, Eunoe benhami n. sp., Eunoe white-tail n. sp.). COI was obtained from 2 specimens, generating an intra-clade uncorrected p-distance of 0.02%. Among the taxa sequenced for this study, Eunoe sp_4 sp nov was found to be closely related to Eunoe sp from 1343 m in the southwest Indian Ocean (Serpetti et al., 2012) and seprated from that species by an uncorrected COI p-distance of 6%.

The papillae on the lateral margin are more conspicuous since the posterior papillae are much less numerous in a row slightly anterior to the posterior margin - this detail is also clearly noted by Benham: "Near the posterior margin there is a row of widely separated white i.e., unpigmented, and probably transparent in life, long, finger-shaped papillae. These are absent on the first elytron. On the anterior elytra there may be as many as eight of these soft papillae; on the majority I note some 4-6, while on the posterior ones only three are present." (Benham, 1915: 198). This describes exactly the elytra of the new specimen from the Great Australian Bight. Eunoe etheridgei is not closely related to other species of Eunoe or other Polynoinae seen in this study; the closest taxon (uncorrected COI p-distance 18%) is Antipathipolyeunoa sp from 312 m in the Coral Sea

325.text: Eunoe leiotentaculata, originally described from South of New Zealand at 1100–1200 m (Averincev, 1878) is now recorded widely in the south Pacific-New Zealand-southern Australia at depths of 549-1371 m. Eunoe leiotentaculata can be identified from other species in this study using the key provided. The long dorsal cirri, extended bare tip region of the neurochaetae and distinctive mauve pigmentation on in a band on the psterior margin of the elytra are distinctive characters for recognition. Maximum intra-clade uncorrected COI p-distances for this species were 2.5% and 2.8%, greater than for most other species for which COI data were available in this study.

325.text: Harmothoe australis is the only bathyal-abyssal polynoid from the Australian region with elytral soft papilae on the dorsal surface (as against hard micro- or macrotubercles) and with entire (smooth) elytral margins and with neuropodial supra-acicular process present. originally described from the Great Australian Bight from 1320-1340 m, H. australis is now recorded widely along the southern coast of Australia from 913-4035 m. Kirkegaard describes the elytra more accurately than he figures them: "Elytra without marginal or surface papillae but with small tubercles on lateral part and a few larger globular tubercles on posterior part of the surface." (Kirkegaard, 1995: 12, fig. 6d). The neurochaetae "Some neurosetae are unidentate and other have a small secondary thin tooth beneath the main fang" (Kirkegaard, 1995: 13, fig. 6c) are indeed distinctive (our fig. xxxx). A COI sequence was only obtained from one specimen so intraspecific genetic distance value is not available.

325.text: These specimens most resemble Lagisca longipalpa Kirkegaard 1995, because of the combination of mostly unidentate neurochaetae, the form of spination of noto- and neurochaetae, presence of papillae on antennae, tentacular and dorsal cirri, presence of notochaetae on tentaculophores, and the forms of elytral ornamentation (marginal and surface papillae, conical and cylindrical tubercles with truncate tips and a few larger inflated bell-shaped macrotubercles). Some neurochaetae are indistinctly bidentate with a raised area appearing like an abraded secondary tooth (Kirkegaard, 1995: Figure 8d, our figure nnn). The palps are not as long as those of Kirkegaard’s specimens however, and he describes them as smooth, which may be due to the very small size and sparseness of these papillae, only visible under high magnification with low-incident light. Authors frequently describe Polynoidae species with smooth palps although in our experience no polynoid lacks palpal papillae entirely although papillae are frequently very small and sparse and only observed with careful observation - (see also R.Barnich, pers. comm.). Other differences can probably be put down to Kirkegaard's incomplete description and figures. His parapodium figure is unclear, nor is this structure described in the text; the text does describe small cephalic peaks but thse are not visible in his Figure 8a. Other similar species are H. crosetensis (McIntosh, 1885) and Lagisca antarctica McIntosh 1885, but the former differs from this species due to the lack of posterior patch of elytral macrotubercles, and the latter lacks the longer cylindrical tubercles with crown-like tips of the present species. Because of the relative lack of bidentate neurochaetae from most parapodia along the body, the species can be readily confused with Eunoe species, however it is distinguished by the form of the neuropodial tips – not strongly unidentate nor strongly falcate as in most Eunoe species. Lagisca longipalpa has been previously recorded only from southwest New Zealand waters in 3580 m depth. We consider this species to be Harmothoe longipalpa comb. nov. since only the largest specimen may have up to 10 posterior segments lacking elytra among material that otherwise fits within Harmothoe. We do not consider this a sufficient basis for recognising a genus distinct from Harmothoe for this species. Our data agrees with the conclusion of other authors (Pettibone, 1953, 1963; Tebble & Chambers, 1982; Chambers and Muir (1997; Barnich & Fiege, 2000; Barnich & Fiege, 2009) in that specimens of "Lagisca" appear to be large examples of species of Harmothoe and that Lagisca Malmgren, 1865 should be considered a junior synonym of Harmothoe Kinberg, 1856

325.text: Harmothoe paxtoni was described from off the southern tip of Tasmania from 1800 m (Averincev, 1878). The specimens reported here, from 1168-1342 m in the Great Australian Bight, are the first record of the species since the original description. Averincev (1978) did not note host association but the new material reported here was commensal in ambulacral grooves of asteroids Benthopecten munidae Clark, 1969. Eunoe bathydomus (Ditlevsen, 1917) from the North Atlantic is similar morphologically and genetically and is commensal on several species of Holothuroidea. Maximum intra-clade genetic distance for Harmothoe paxtoni is less than 0.01% (uncorrected COI p-distance; although COI could not be obtained from one specimen, NMV F271044). Corresponding inter-clade distances from the most similar species, Eunoe benhami sp. nov. (from this study) and E. bathydomus are 4.2% and 7.3% respectively. Harmothoe paxtoni can be distinguished from other Australian abyssal and bathya- polynoids in this study using the key.

325.text: [some of the following has duplication that needs to be removed] The distinction between Lagisca and Harmothoe relies largely on the presence of a long posterior section of the body lacking elytra (in Lagisca) whereas this extended posterior section is absent in Harmothoe species. Whether this is a valid taxonomic character has been disputed in recent studies – it has been suggested that species referable to Lagisca are simply very large individuals of Harmothoe species which have grown additional posterior segments (Barnich & Fiege 2000, Barnich pers. Comm.). Pettibone (1953) synonymised the type species of Lagisca, L. rarispina (Sars, 1861), with Harmothoe extenuata. Salazar-Silva (2006) considered Lagisca a valid taxon while Barnich & Fiege (2009) moved several species from Harmothoe to Lagisca and doubted the validity of Lagisca. In our study, several large specimens of Harmothoe paxtoni also had additional posterior segments bare of elytra which would cause them to be arbitrarily treated as belonging to Lagisca. Aside from having a few additional posterior segments (consistent with their large size: up to 45 segments rather than 37-39 in most Harmothoe we can find no differences between "Lagisca torbeni" which we here refer to Harmothoe torbeni (Kirkegaard, 1995) comb. nov. In assigning Lagisca torbeni Kirkegaard 1995 to Harmothoe torbeni (Kirkegaard 1995) n. comb. we follow Barnich et al 2009 who suggested that Lagisca is based on large specimens of Harmothoe spp which have added posterior segments during growth, creating a posterior section of 10-14 segments lacking elytra (the definition of Lagisca). Nor do our own ML trees [insert fig refs] support Lagisca as a monophyletic group. The description provided here completes and clarifies several characters that were unclear or not stated in the original description, including pharynx and jaws which were not visible to Kirkegaard. Kirkegaard (1995: 16) states "Neuropodia with a long digitiform process ... " but his figure 9 does not show a supra-acicular process. However as our fig shows, a supra-acicular process is present but it is small and would be easily missed. Kirkegaard states that "Antennae, tentacular cirri and parapodial cirri with small thin papillae" which we could not initially reconcile with our new material from the Great Australian BIght which appeared to lack papillae on all appendages. However at high magnification it is true that as Kirkegaard states, very thin and small papillae are present, although sparse, on all intact antennae, tentacular cirri and parapodial cirri on our specimens. These fine papillae can only be observed under stereo microscopes at high magnification with low-incident angle light. Note also that Kirkegaard 1995 figure 9 only shows lateral antennae and tentacular cirri with papillae; dorsal and ventral cirri (drawn much larger) have no papillae although they are there (in our specimens). In all other respects our material agrees closely with the description of Kirkegaard 1995. Among bathyal-abyssal Polynoidae from southern and eastern Australia, Harmothoe torbeni is readily recognisable by the elytra with hard tubercles and long dense papillae on posterior and lateral regions, the prominent dorsally directed bundles of stout notochaetae and the small but distinct cephalic peaks

325.text: Day (1967: 44) referred Hololepida australis Monro, 1936 to Alentia Malmgren, 1865 and also provided an amended diagnosis of Alentia "to include Hololepida Moore, 1905". Subsequent authors (eg Fauchald, 1977; Imajima, 1997) have retained Hololepida and Alentia as valid genera. Barnich & Fiege (2003: 80) provide an emended diagnosis restricting Alentia to short-bodied species with about 45 segments and 18 pairs of elytra. For these reasons Day's treatment is not accepted here and all long-bodied forms are accepted in Hololepida which now includes 5 species including Hololepida australis Monro, 1936.

325.text: There are currently five species described in the genus Hololepida. All species except H. oculata Monro, 1936 are reported as having neuropodial supra-acicular process absent. These specimens are most similar to H. oculata Hartman, 1967 and H. australis Monro, 1936 and appear to have a combination of their characters. The presence of confluent eyes, a facial tubercle that is conical and projecting, and lateral antennae that are inserted terminally on the prostomial lobes are indicative of H. australis, whereas the presence of a neuropodial supra-acicular process (cf. absent in H. australis), lateral antennae bases that touch basally (or appear almost fused) indicate their affinity with H. oculata. Until better specimens complete with elytra as well as full body segments with a corresponding full complement of elytra (and not reduced due to regenerating posterior end) are found, and also Hartman’s type specimen of H. oculata can be examined and more details are elucidated, we are tentatively referring these specimens to H. oculata Hartman, 1967

Ventral cirri on 2nd segment (buccal cirrus) elongate, as long as ventral tentacular cirri, larger than subsequent ventral cirri. Some dorsal cirri with elongate cirrophores, styles basally swollen, others tapering evenly, longer than parapodia, much longer posteriorly. Dorsal tubercles nodular. Pair of pygidial cirri elongate, cirriform. Also observed from males: Some small brown pigment spots present on dorsum, prostomium and ventrum, on some specimens. Pharynx with 2 pairs of jaws, dorsally fused and ventrally fused, smooth falcate, without lateral teeth; with 9 pairs terminal papillae, none enlarged. Small nephridial papillae present ventrally from segment 5

7.text: Excluded from Intkey. Probable synonym of Harmothoe fide Barnich & Fiege 2000: 1915. No modern diagnosis distinguishes Harmothoe and Lagisca.

21.text: Specimens of Harmothoe extenuata have often been referred to the genus Lagisca Malmgren, 1865 by various authors (e.g. Fauvel, 1923; Hartmann-Schroeder, 1996), due to the presence of several uncovered last segments in large specimens and the notochaetae being only slightly stouter than the neurochaetae. In accordance with Pettibone (1953, 1963), Tebble and Chambers (1982), and "Chambers and Muir (1997) we consider these characters not of generic importance, especially since large specimens of other Harmothoe species also show an uncovered tail (see ® gure 1), and the diOEerence in thickness of chaetae is di� cult to evaluate. Since Pettibone (1953) synonymized the type species of the genus Lagisca, L. rarispina (Sars, 1861), with H. extenuata, we doubt the validity of the genus Lagisca, being aware that only a complete revision of both genera could bring enough evidence for this hypothesis.' (Barnich & Fiege, 2000: 1915)

325.text: based on the multidentate neurochaetae which are strikingly similar to those seen in Gorekia crassicirris (Willey, 1902), it seems likely that Lepidogyra alba Hartman, 1967 is a junior synonym of Gorekia crassicirris (Willey, 1902). Both species are known only from the Antarctic and the form of multidentate neurochaetae they share is not seen in any other Polynoid. Hartman (1967) described Lepidogyra as being a lepidonotin with antennae continuous with the prostomial lobe but Kristian Fauchald re-examined the type material on 5 Mar 2001 and recorded lateral antennae as being terminoventrally inserted. Kristian also noted the type material to be in poor condition and that may have been true also when Hartman's origiinal description was made. Lepidogyra alba has not been collected since the original description, but Gorekia crassicirris was collected in commensal relationship with echinoids by Schiaparelli et al (2011) who provided a redescription including live photographs. We consider the two species to be con-specific and Lepidogyra Hartman, 1967 to be a junior synonym of Gorekia Bergström, 1916.

325.text: This specimen most resembles M. violacea (Levinsen, 1886), which has only been recorded from the Arctic and North Atlantic Ocean. Several other species that possess small or indistinct frontal filaments, and also bear some resemblance to the specimen include M. macintoshi Neal, Brasier & Wiklund 2018, from southern Africa, M. australis Wu & Wang, 1987, from the 'Southern Ocean', M. clarionensis Bonifacio & Menot 2018 and M. parvafauces Bonifacio & Menot 2018, both from the equatorial eastern Pacific Ocean, and M. patersoni Neal Brasier & Wiklund 2018 and M. brenesorum Neal Brasier & Wiklund 2018, both from Pine Island Bay, Amundsen Sea, Southern Ocean. However, these species all differ from the specimen described herein by the following features: M. macintoshi was described by Neal, Brasier & Wiklund (2018) from old material collected by McIntosh in 540–900 m depth off South Africa, and originally identified as Polynoe (Macellicephala) mirabilis by McIntosh (1905). Although this resembles our specimen strongly due to its dorsal purple colouration, it possesses frontal filaments that are short, slender and prominent (not papilla-like), conical dorsal tubercles (not digitiform), neurochaetae with faint serration on both margins tapering to pointed tips (not curved/slightly hooked; nor faint serrations along one side only) and smooth copper-coloured notochaetae. Also, as there are no sequences for this species in GenBank due to the age of the material, there was no basis for molecular comparison with our specimen. Similarly, sequences for M. australis Wu & Wang, 1987, have not been submitted to GenBank either. However, although our specimen also resembles this latter species in some respects, M. australis possesses neurochaetae that distally taper abruptly to slightly hooked tips whereas our specimen’s neurochaetae are evenly tapered and tips are pointed, appearing slightly curved/hooked only when viewed laterally; also the frontal filaments of M. australis are 'minute, indistinct' (Wu & Wang, 1987), whereas this specimen possesses small papilla-like frontal filaments; and M. australis also lacks dorsal tubercles. M. clarionensis possesses neurochaetae with minutely bidentate tips. M. parvafauces possesses very small jaws and lacks strong purple-coloured pigment, even when live. M. patersoni Neal Brasier & Wiklund, 2018 lacks dorsal tubercles, and possesses neurochaetae with bidentate tips. M. brenesorum Neal Brasier & Wiklund, 2018 has distinct and slender frontal filaments (not papilla-like), dorsal tubercles as distinct conical mounds (not digitiform), ventral cirri that are 'short' (not extremely short), and neurochaetae with serrations along both sides and pointed tips (not curved/hooked) Anna, I've deleted this, there is precedent for wide, even global distributions in abyssal spp: ", but it is unlikely that our specimen belongs to this species due to such great geographical distance". Also, if "This specimen most resembles M. violacea (Levinsen, 1886)", why are we calling it "Macellicephala cf macintoshi"?!

325.text: Due to the absence of lateral antennae, this specimen is assigned to Macellicephalinae, and appears to belong to the group of genera also lacking a median antenna (Anantennata clade of Bonifacio & Menot, 2018) which includes species of Bruunilla, Hodor, Nu, Polaruschakov, Diplaconotum, Bathymariana, Bathymiranda, Bathycanadia and Bathyedithia. It most resembles a species of Bathyedithia, because of such features as jaws that are serrated (cf. Polaruschakov, Diplaconotum, Bathymiranda, and Bathycanadia which possess smooth jaws), nine pairs of elytrophores (cf. Bathymariana with 11 pairs), presence of notochaetae (cf. Nu where they are absent), similar unmodified neurochaetae on all chaetigers (cf. Hodor in which they are modified on segments 3–7), achaetous tentacular segment (cf. Bathymiranda), and lack of neuropodial papillae (cf. Diplaconotum). Bonifacio & Menot (2018) emended the generic diagnosis for Bathyedithia, to include a range in the number of elytra pairs (9–10) and the number of pharyngeal terminal papillae (7–9 pairs) both of which were previously thought to be fixed characters for most Macellicephalinae genera. Because we cannot determine the number of pairs of pharyngeal papillae, and because of some dissimilarities with other features of previously described species of Bathyedithia such as chaetal form, we are tentative about the determination of this single specimen. RW notes: The definition of Bathyedithia by Bonifacio & Menot (2018) encompasses taxa with 25 or 26 segments, 9 or 10 pairs of elytra, cephalic peaks present or absent, dorsal tubercles either absent or present on chaetiger 6 (segment 7) only, suggesting that the current members of Bathyedithia do not comprise a monophyletic group. The genus comprises 4 species including the present one [Macellicephalinae sp5] but only two species have molecular sequence data: ours and Bathyedithia retierei Bonifacio & Menot, 2018. Our molecular analaysis shows that our species and Bathyedithia retierei Bonifacio & Menot, 2018 are unrelated [insert COI genetic distance] and further supports the conclusion that Bathyedithia comprises more than one natural group and is in need of revision. Since our species and the type species of the genus, Bathyedithia berkeleyi (Levenstein, 1971) are the only two species in the genus with 26 segments and 9 pairs of elytra, we place our species in Bathyedithia and we suggest that Bathyedithia retierei Bonifácio & Menot, 2018 belongs in a new genus.

325.text: Malmgrenia sp. 7122 is readily distinguished from all other bathyal-abyssal Australian Polynoidae by having nucal flap, bidentate neurochaetae and supra-acicular neuropodial process. Among species of Malmgrenia and similar genera Malmgrenia sp.7122 is closest to Malmgrenia andreapolis McIntosh,1874 from the northeast Atlantic (both with papillate lateral antennae, nuchal flap, supracicular neuropodial process, bidentate neurochaetae). However the two species perhaps differ in the form of the neurochaetae which have less conspicuous secondary teeth (but perhaps are worn) in our specimen and in pigmentation, which is lacking in our specimen. We are not confident to describe our single specimen as a new species without further material.

325.text: Antipathipolyeunoa Pettibone, 1991 was synonymised with Parahololepidella Pettibone, 1969 by Gonzalez et al. (2023a). Besides the characters discussed by Gonzalez et al. (variable presence of chaetae on the tentacular segment, irregular elytral distribution on posterior segments), species of Parahololepidella also differ in respect of the facial tubercle which is absent (a simple tripartite upper lip present) in P. nuttingi and in P. xxx sp. nov while a raised tubercular facial rubercle is present in P. greeffi (Augener, 1918). Parahololepidella now comprises three species including Parahololepidella xxxx sp nov described below from the Great Australian Bight in the Southern Ocean and P. nuttingi (Pettibone, 1991) from the North Atlantic. Serpetti et al. (2017) reported material of Antipathipolyeunoa from the Indian Ocean which presumably represents another species of Parahololepidella but Serpetti et al. did not describe a new species.

325.text: Parahololepidella yilgarn sp. nov. is close to Parahololepidella nuttingi Pettibone, 1991, notably in being a long-bodied Polynoinae with elyta present to near the posterior end, a digitiform subacicular neurpodial process (but no supra-acicular process), long smooth dorsal cirri and having nephridiopores from segment 6. The new species differs in the position of the cephalic peaks, which are clearly drawn by Pettibone as continuous extensions of lateral prostomial margin in P. nuttingi wheras P. GAB1 sp. nov. has distinct cephalic peaks in the middle of the anterior margin of the prostomium. Parahololepidella GAB1 also has much shorter lateral antennae than in P. nuttingi and tips of internal aciculae project prominently from the tentaculophores (Pettibone notes tentaculophores achaetous in A. nuttingi). The other species of Parahololepidella, P. greeffi has an inflated globular facial tubercule compared with a tripartite ridge in Parahololepidella GAB1. Although elytra missing from segments anterior to 13 on all specimens of P. yilgarn, based on Pettobine (1991: FIg. 2 G, H & I), elytra of P. yilgarn appear smaller than those of P. nuttingi. Parahololepidella yilgarn sp. nov is commensal on Parantipathes Brook, 1889 while the other two species in the genus are commensal on a different antipatharian coral genus, Tanacetipathes Opresko, 2001 (Gonzalez et al. 2023a).

325.text: These specimens agree with the emended genus diagnosis by Bonifácio and Menot (2018) for Polaruschakov Pettibone, 1976, because of the absence of all antennae combined with non-dentate jaws (or with a single small secondary marginal tooth) and the absence of flattened scale-like structures on segment 6, but, because of their small size, damaged bodies and posterior ends and missing elytra, they could not be identified to species. There are five species in this genus which has only been reported from deep Arctic waters, off the Mediterranean (in Pettibone 1976) and in abyssal waters of the equatorial eastern Pacific Ocean off Mexico (Bonifácio and Menot 2018). This species exhibits small morphological differences to the five previously described Polaruschakov species (WoRMs June 2023) - P. polaris (Uschakov, 1957), P. reyssi Pettibone 1976, P. lamellae Bonifacio & Menot 2018, P. limaae Bonifacio & Menot 2018, and P. omnesae Bonifacio & Mento 2018. It bears most resemblance to P. polaris because of the similar number of segments, the similar number of notochaetae per parapodium, and shape of prostomium, but differs due to the presence of 2 different types of neurochaetae (blunt and pointed, compared to blunt-tipped only in P. polaris), and because this latter species has only been recorded from North Atlantic (Arctic) waters, it is unlikely to be the same species as our species descibed herein. P. limaae (recorded from the equatorial Eastern Pacific Ocean) has 2 types neurochaetae, but differs from P. investigator by the shape of the prostomium (short and conical anteriorly), the very much reduced notopodia, the much fewer number of notochaetae (1–2), and the presence of a ventral pygidial papilla. P. investigator differs from P. reyssi (recorded from the Mediterranean) which has notochaetae with capillary tips, and from P. omnesae (recorded from the equatorial Eastern Pacific Ocean) which has conical prostomial lobes, short palps and tentacular cirri (reaching only to segment 3), few notochaetae (1–3 per parapodium), and neurochaetae with pointed tips only. It shares 2 kinds of neurochaetae with P. lamellae (recorded from the equatorial Eastern Pacific Ocean) but differs from it by the lack of lamelliform dorsal tubercles on elytrigerous segments. The occurrence or absence of large flattened structures dorsally on segment 6, which these specimens exhibit, is now considered a possible reproductive feature, according to Bonifacio & Menot (2018), as presence or absence ("without pattern") may occur in "other taxa belonging to the Anantennata clade". Also, the number of segments in the genus Polaruschakov appears to vary with size (age), and very small specimens may only possess 15–17 segments. Polaruschakov investigator sp. nov.xxx from P. lamellae, P. omnesae and P. limaae (it’s 3 geographically closest congenors). This is the first record of a Polaruschakov species from the southern hemisphere.

325.text: Polyeunoa laevis is included in the Australian bathyal-abyssal fauna on the basis of specimens in the AM and USNM from the vicinity of Macquarie Island in 787-1000 m. The maximum depth recorded for this species is 2980 m (from the Falkland Islands) but that is not typical - of ~350 records from Hartman, 1967, Pettibone, 1969 and Barnich et al., 2012 (via USNM collections online and GBIF), only 9 are deeper than 2,000 m. Most records are from 50-500 m, although this is clearly confounded, but to an unkown degree, by sampling biases (Higgs & Attrill 2015; Hughes et al 2021).

13.text: Coding here for Polynoinae is based on the very broad concept of Barnich & Fiege, 2003. Coding for Polynoinae sensu Wehe, 2006 (based on the combined concepts of Acholoinae and Polynoinae of Hanley, 1989) would not be useful and probably not diagnosably different since the following qualified descriptors would have to be coded as present or absent: Elytra often 15 pairs; elytra usually with tubercles or papillae; dirsal cirri usually with papillate stynes; dorsal tubercles usually distinct; Neurpoodial acicular lobe often with supra-acicular process; notochaetae and neurochaetae usually numerous.
